nameStory: The ruby-throated hummingbird gets its name from the brilliant ruby-red throat patch, called a gorget, that adorns the male birds. This iridescent red throat shimmers like a precious gemstone when it catches the light, making it look like the bird is wearing a tiny ruby necklace.
description: The ruby-throated hummingbird is a tiny, jewel-like bird about the size of a large bee or small moth. Males sport that famous ruby-red throat that gives the species its name, while females have white throats with subtle markings. Both sexes have emerald-green backs that shimmer in sunlight and wings that beat so fast they create a distinctive humming sound. These remarkable little birds typically measure about 3-4 inches long with a wingspan of roughly 4 inches.

idTips.label: Ruby-red throat (males)
idTips.description: Adult males display an iridescent ruby-red throat patch that can appear black in poor light but blazes like a tiny flame when the angle is right

idTips.label: Humming wing sound
idTips.description: Wings beat 50-80 times per second, creating a distinctive soft humming or buzzing sound that you'll hear before you see the bird

idTips.label: Emerald-green back
idTips.description: Both males and females have brilliant metallic green backs and crowns that shimmer like wet paint in sunlight

idTips.label: Hovering flight pattern
idTips.description: Unique ability to hover motionless in mid-air, fly backwards, and dart in any direction with rapid, jerky movements

idTips.label: Needle-like bill
idTips.description: Straight, thin black bill about as long as the head, perfectly designed for reaching into tubular flowers

idTips.label: White throat patch (females)
idTips.description: Female birds have clean white throats sometimes dotted with tiny dark speckles, lacking the male's ruby gorget

habitat: Ruby-throated hummingbirds thrive in gardens, woodland edges, parks, and anywhere with abundant flowers, especially tubular blooms like bee balm, cardinal flower, and trumpet vine. They're particularly drawn to areas with both nectar sources and small insects, often seen around feeders, flowering trees, and shrubs. You'll find them from sea level to mountain elevations throughout New England, especially in areas that offer both open feeding spaces and nearby trees for nesting.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive first in late April to early May, establishing territories around the best nectar sources. Look for aggressive territorial displays and the first visits to fresh hummingbird feeders.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season with breeding, nest-building, and constant feeding. Young birds appear in mid to late summer, identifiable by their smaller size and less vibrant coloring.
seasonality.fall: Migration begins in late August through September, with birds building up fat reserves for their incredible journey south. This is often when feeders see the most activity.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having migrated to Central America, Mexico, and Florida. A rare straggler might linger into early winter during warm years.

funFact: Despite weighing less than a penny, ruby-throated hummingbirds migrate across the Gulf of Mexico in a single non-stop flight of over 500 miles, doubling their body weight beforehand to fuel this incredible 18-20 hour journey over open water.
confusionNotes: Ruby-throated hummingbirds are the only breeding hummingbird species in New England, so any hummingbird you see here in summer is almost certainly this species. Occasionally, western hummingbird species appear as rare vagrants, but the ruby-throat's combination of ruby-red male throat and emerald-green back is diagnostic in our region.
contextualKnowledge: Many people think hummingbirds only eat nectar, but they actually get about half their nutrition from tiny insects and spiders, which provide essential proteins. The 'hummingbird' name comes from the sound of their rapidly beating wings, not from any vocal humming sounds they make.
compareHints: The ruby-throated hummingbird is most closely related to the black-chinned hummingbird of the western United States, but that species has a black throat with purple lower border rather than the all-ruby throat. In New England, ruby-throats are unmistakable as our only resident hummingbird species, though rare vagrant western species might occasionally appear during migration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (the only regular hummingbird in New England) have males with solid ruby-red throats that flash like neon signs, Black-chinned males show the distinctive two-toned black and purple throat combination.
